analysis.one_liner: Strips the Federal Reserve's power to lend emergency funds directly to private companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced days after Lehman's collapse and the AIG rescue, drew no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted the section of the Federal Reserve Act that lets the Fed lend money directly to private companies — not just banks — when they cannot get credit anywhere else and circumstances are dire. That power is what allowed the Fed to rescue firms like AIG in the fall of 2008. Sen. Jim Bunning, a longtime Fed critic, introduced it on September 17, 2008, and it went nowhere: no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, taxpayers and ordinary borrowers would have been protected from the Fed directly backstopping private firms with public credit. But it would have also removed the tool the Fed uses to stop a credit freeze from spreading to jobs and everyday lending, so the benefit is genuinely two-sided.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Federal Reserve's authority to discount notes for 'private individuals, partnerships, or corporations unable to secure adequate credit accommodations from other banking institutions' — the emergency lending power used to support firms like AIG that are not ordinary banks.

By deleting that paragraph of Section 13 of the Federal Reserve Act, the bill would bar the Fed from making discount-rate funds available to non-bank private firms, ending direct Fed rescues of companies that got themselves into trouble.

analysis.who_pays: In a future financial panic, the Fed could no longer lend directly to a failing firm to stop a collapse from cascading — the cost would fall on workers and businesses who depend on functioning credit markets if a crisis turns into a freeze.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone relying on credit during a crisis

drawbacks.text: The emergency lending power this bill removes is the tool the Fed used during the 2008 panic to prevent individual firm failures from freezing the entire credit system; stripping it in the middle of that very crisis would have left the Fed without a way to stop a domino collapse, a risk to jobs and ordinary lending.

The bill was a one-sentence repeal with no replacement framework, no hearing, and no cosponsors — even lawmakers who shared concerns about Fed bailouts offered no support, suggesting it was a statement of principle rather than workable legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument on each side. Blocking the Fed from lending public money directly to private companies protects taxpayers from bearing private firms' losses. But the same power is how the Fed prevented a cascading credit collapse in 2008, and removing it entirely — with nothing to replace it, mid-crisis — could have made panics worse for everyone. The bill offered no middle path, such as lending with taxpayer reimbursement requirements or congressional approval.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Bunning introduced the bill on September 17, 2008, two days after the Federal Reserve's emergency rescue of AIG and one day after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The committee took no action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill never reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Federal Reserve kept its emergency lending authority intact, and large financial firms retained access to direct Fed support during the ongoing crisis. No one acted to advance the bill, so the outcome simply preserved the powers that existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Fed and Wall Street firms it backs

for.name: Jim Bunning
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 17, 2008 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from it; the sole sponsor was a Republican who had long criticized the Fed.

industries.industry: Large financial firms (non-bank companies relying on Fed emergency credit)
industries.note: By dying, the bill left intact the Fed's power to lend directly to private firms in trouble — the authority behind the AIG rescue. Those firms keep a public backstop for private losses that ordinary people ultimately underwrite.
The bill would have trimmed the Fed's authority; its death left the central bank's crisis powers untouched, including the ability to act without congressional approval.

The repealed provision is aimed at firms 'unable to secure adequate credit accommodations from other banking institutions' — its removal would leave banks as the Fed's lending channel, but in a panic banks benefit from any tool that stops a systemic freeze.
